propositions.text: On October 17, 2009, the Ocean Lady was apprehended off Vancouver Island with 76 Tamil passengers from Sri Lanka seeking refugee status without legal documentation.
propositions.quote: On October 17, 2009, a vessel called the Ocean Lady was apprehended off the west coast of Vancouver Island, in British Columbia. Seventy-six people, among them the appellants, were aboard. All were Tamils from Sri Lanka. They claimed to have fled Sri Lanka because their lives were endangered in the aftermath of the civil war in that country. They asked for refugee status in Canada. None had the required legal documentation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that on October 17, 2009, the Ocean Lady was apprehended with 76 Tamil asylum-seekers from Sri Lanka lacking legal documentation.

propositions.text: The Crown claims the four appellants were organizers of the voyage and that most passengers paid $30,000 to $40,000 for it.
propositions.quote: The Crown claims that the four appellants — the captain and chief crew of the vessel — were the organizers of the venture. The Crown alleges that the majority of passengers each paid, or promised to pay, $30,000 to $40,000 for the voyage.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown alleges the four appellants organized the voyage and passengers paid $30,000 to $40,000 each, says the respondent.

propositions.text: The appellants were charged under s. 117 of IRPA, which criminalizes organizing or aiding illegal entry into Canada, with serious consequences.
propositions.quote: The appellants were charged under s. 117 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 (“IRPA ”), which makes it an offence to “organize, induce, aid or abet” the coming into Canada of people in contravention of the IRPA . Consequences of conviction could include lengthy imprisonment and disqualification from consideration as a refugee.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellants were charged under s. 117 IRPA for organizing illegal entry, with serious penalties.

propositions.text: The appellants challenged s. 117 IRPA as unconstitutional for infringing s. 7 Charter rights to life, liberty and security.
propositions.quote: Before their trial, the appellants challenged the constitutionality of s. 117 of the IRPA , on the ground that it infringes the right to life, liberty and security of the person enshrined in s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms .

propositions.text: The trial judge ruled s. 117 unconstitutional for criminalizing helping family and humanitarian aid, but the Court of Appeal reversed and found it constitutional.
propositions.quote: The trial judge ruled that the provision was unconstitutional because it criminalized not only organized people smuggling, but helping close family members to come to Canada and humanitarian assistance to refugees. The British Columbia Court of Appeal reversed that decision, and found the provision to be constitutional.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argued s. 117 infringed s. 7 Charter rights; the trial judge agreed but the Court of Appeal reversed that finding.

propositions.text: Section 117 is unconstitutional insofar as it permits prosecution for humanitarian aid, mutual assistance among asylum-seekers, or family assistance.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I conclude that, insofar as s. 117 permits prosecution for humanitarian aid to undocumented entrants, mutual assistance amongst asylum-seekers or assistance to family members, it is unconstitutional.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 117 is unconstitutional when it permits prosecution for humanitarian aid, mutual assistance, or family help.

propositions.text: Canadian authorities intercepted the Ocean Lady with 76 Tamil asylum-seekers from Indonesia and Thailand, none with proper documentation, most paying $30,000 to $40,000.
propositions.quote: Canadian authorities intercepted the freighter ship Ocean Lady offshore of Vancouver Island. They found 76 passengers aboard; all were Tamil asylum-seekers from Sri Lanka who had boarded the ship in Southeast Asia: 24 boarded the ship in Indonesia between June and August 2009, and 52 in Thailand in September 2009. None of the 76 migrants had the proper documentation to enter Canada. Most had agreed to pay a sum of between $30,000 and $40,000 to come to Canada. Typically, down payments of $5,000 were exacted prior to boarding, together with undertaking a debt of another $25,000 to $35,000 to be paid subsequent to arrival in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states authorities intercepted the Ocean Lady with 76 Tamil asylum-seekers from Southeast Asia lacking documentation, most paying $30,000-$40,000.

propositions.text: The four appellants are alleged organizers and chief crew of a for-profit smuggling operation from Southeast Asia to Canada.
propositions.quote: The four appellants, Francis Anthonimuthu Appulonappa, Hamalraj Handasamy, Jeyachandran Kanagarajah and Vignarajah Thevarajah, are alleged to have been the point persons for a transnational for-profit operation to smuggle undocumented migrants from Southeast Asia to Canada. They are said to have been responsible for organizing the asylum-seekers in Indonesia and Thailand prior to boarding the freighter, and serving as the chief crew of the ship on the voyage to Canada — Mr. Handasamy as captain, Mr. Thevarajah as chief engineer, and Mr. Kanagarajah and Mr. Appulonappa as key crew members.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellants allegedly organized and crewed a for-profit smuggling operation from Southeast Asia to Canada.

propositions.text: The appellants were charged under s. 117 IRPA, which prohibits knowingly organizing or aiding entry of persons without required documents.
propositions.quote: The appellants were charged with the offence of “Organizing entry into Canada” found in s. 117 of the IRPA , which, at the relevant time, provided: 117. (1) No person shall knowingly organize, induce, aid or abet the coming into Canada of one or more persons who are not in possession of a visa, passport or other document required by this Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellants were charged under s. 117 IRPA prohibiting organizing or aiding undocumented entry.

propositions.text: IRPA s. 117 was amended in 2012; the version at the time of the offences is no longer in force and its constitutionality is not before the court.
propositions.quote: The IRPA was amended by the Protecting Canada’s Immigration System Act, S.C. 2012, c. 17, ss. 41(1) and 41(4) , whereby s. 117(1) was replaced by a new subsection and two subsections were added, which came into force on December 15, 2012. Section 117 as it was at the time of the alleged offences of the appellants is therefore no longer in force. The constitutionality of the current s. 117 is not before us.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 117 IRPA was amended in 2012; the earlier version is no longer in force and current constitutionality is not at issue.

propositions.text: The appellants applied for a declaration that s. 117 is overbroad and unconstitutional for potentially convicting humanitarian workers or family members.
propositions.quote: The appellants brought an application before Silverman J. on a voir dire for a declaration that s. 117 of the IRPA is unconstitutionally overbroad. They did not contend that s. 117 is unconstitutional as it applies to the allegations against them, which are that they were part of a for-profit smuggling operation. However, they argued that s. 117 is unconstitutional because it may lead to the conviction of humanitarian workers or family members assisting asylum-seekers for altruistic reasons. They argued that convicting people in these categories exceeds the legislative intent of s. 117 and infringes the guarantee of liberty contrary to the principle of fundamental justice against overbreadth. This violation of the liberty guarantee in s. 7 of the Charter was not justified under s. 1 of the Charter , they submitted.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argued s. 117 is overbroad and unconstitutional for potentially convicting humanitarian or family helpers, says the applicant.

propositions.text: The Crown accepted s. 117 was not meant to convict family or humanitarian aid but argued s. 117(4) requiring Attorney General consent prevents overbreadth.
propositions.quote: The Crown accepted that the purpose of s. 117 was not to convict persons helping close family members come to Canada or persons providing legitimate humanitarian aid to people coming to Canada. However, it argued that this did not render s. 117 overbroad because s. 117(4) of the IRPA required that the Attorney General of Canada authorize prosecution, which would allow him to screen out people in these categories.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown accepted s. 117 was not meant to convict family or humanitarian aid but said Attorney General consent prevents overbreadth, says the respondent.

propositions.text: Silverman J. found s. 117 overbroad and unconstitutional as it permits prosecution of humanitarian and family aid, and Attorney General consent does not save it.
propositions.quote: Silverman J. concluded that, as the Crown contended, the purpose of s. 117 does not extend to prosecution of genuine humanitarian aid workers or family members. Because s. 117 permits the prosecution of such persons, it violates the s. 7 guarantee of liberty in a way that is overbroad, and hence not in accord with the principles of fundamental justice. Silverman J. held that s. 117 could not be interpreted or “read down” to make it Charter compliant and that the prior consent to prosecution required by s. 117(4) does not save s. 117 from being unconstitutionally overbroad. Nor, in his view, was the overbreadth justified under s. 1 of the Charter . Silverman J. therefore declared s. 117 of the IRPA to be inconsistent with s. 7 of the Charter and hence of no force or effect under s. 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982 . He ordered that the indictments of the appellants be quashed: 2013 BCSC 198.

paragraphs.summary: Silverman J. found s. 117 overbroad and unconstitutional for prosecuting humanitarian and family aid; Attorney General consent does not save it.

propositions.text: Before the Court of Appeal, the Crown argued s. 117 aims to prevent all organizing or assisting unlawful entry, including family and humanitarian aid, to protect Canadian interests.
propositions.quote: Before the Court of Appeal, the Crown changed its submission on the purpose of s. 117 of the IRPA . It submitted that s. 117 was enacted to prevent all organizing or assisting of unlawful entry of others into Canada, including assistance to close family members and humanitarian assistance. This, the Crown said, was required to further Canada’s goals of (1) controlling who enters its territory; (2) protecting the health, safety, and security of Canadians; (3) preserving the integrity and efficacy of Canada’s lawful immigration and refugee claims regimes; and (4) promoting international justice and cooperation with other states on matters of security.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argued s. 117 aims to prevent all unlawful entry assistance, including family and humanitarian aid, to protect Canadian interests.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal accepted the Crown's revised purpose and held s. 117 constitutional, rejecting exceptions for humanitarian workers.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal accepted this revised submission as the purpose of s. 117 of the IRPA and on that basis held it to be constitutional. Neilson J.A. (Bennett and Hinkson JJ.A. concurring) concluded that Canadian laws criminalizing assistance to undocumented migrants have not historically allowed exceptions based on the offender’s motive or other characteristics. When the provision at issue was enacted in 1988, the question of whether humanitarian workers should be exempted received attention, but Parliament, concerned about “definitional difficulties” and “loopholes”, rejected creating an exception for these groups: para. 107. The purpose of s. 117 therefore aligned with its reach, and the provision was not overbroad.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal accepted the Crown's purpose and held s. 117 constitutional, rejecting humanitarian exceptions.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal held Attorney General consent guards against improper prosecutions, not overbreadth of s. 117(1).
propositions.quote: The court added that the s. 117(4) requirement of the Attorney General’s consent to prosecute would guard against improper prosecutions on humanitarian grounds, family grounds or other grounds. If the Attorney General were to authorize prosecution of people assisting close family members or providing humanitarian assistance, the vice would not be overbreadth of s. 117(1), but the improper exercise of ministerial discretion under s. 117(4) .

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal held Attorney General consent guards against improper prosecutions, not overbreadth of s. 117(1).

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, overturned invalidity declaration, set aside acquittals, and remitted for trial.
propositions.quote: In the result, the Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, overturned the declaration of invalidity, set aside the acquittals and remitted the matter for trial.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, overturned invalidity, set aside acquittals, and remitted for trial.

propositions.text: The IRPA governs immigration and refugee protection, aiming for fair procedures and upholding human rights, supported by international conventions.
propositions.quote: The IRPA (relevant provisions set out in Appendix A) is a complex statute dealing with the entry into Canada of foreign nationals through two processes — the immigration process and the refugee protection process. We are here concerned primarily with the refugee protection process. The IRPA aims to establish “fair and efficient [refugee] procedures that will maintain the integrity of the Canadian refugee protection system, while upholding Canada’s respect for the human rights and fundamental freedoms of all human beings”: s. 3(2)(e). Both goals are underpinned by Canada’s adhesion to international conventions and protocols, discussed more fully below.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains IRPA governs immigration and refugee protection, aiming for fair procedures and human rights, supported by international conventions.

propositions.text: IRPA addresses unauthorized entry threats by sanctioning those who help others enter Canada without required documents.
propositions.quote: A significant concern for the integrity of Canada’s refugee protection system is the threat posed to it by the entry to Canada of unauthorized persons outside the lawful refugee regime. As part of combating this threat, the IRPA contains two provisions which sanction individuals for helping others to enter Canada without the documents required by border authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA sanctions those who help unauthorized persons enter Canada without required documents to protect refugee system integrity.

propositions.text: Section 37(1)(b) renders inadmissible those engaged in transnational people smuggling; s. 117 creates an offence for organizing entry without required documents.
propositions.quote: Section 37(1) (b) of the IRPA renders a person inadmissible to Canada where the person has “engag[ed], in the context of transnational crime”, in people smuggling, and, in effect, prevents that person’s refugee claim from being determined on its merits. Section 117 , under the marginal note “Organizing entry into Canada”, creates an offence. At the relevant time, it read: 117. (1) No person shall knowingly organize, induce, aid or abet the coming into Canada of one or more persons who are not in possession of a visa, passport or other document required by this Act.[1]

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 37(1)(b) renders inadmissible people smugglers; s. 117 creates an offence for organizing entry without documents.

propositions.text: Sections 117(2) and (3) provide penalties; s. 121(1)(c) considers profit as an aggravating factor in sentencing under s. 117.
propositions.quote: Sections 117(2) and 117(3) provide penalties of imprisonment and fines. At the time of the charges at issue in this case, s. 121(1) (c) of the IRPA under the marginal note “Aggravating factors”, stipulated that committing the offence for profit was a fact to be considered in sentencing under s. 117 .[2]

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 117(2) and (3) provide penalties and s. 121(1)(c) considers profit an aggravating sentencing factor.

propositions.text: Subsection (4) provides a screening mechanism for instituting proceedings under s. 117 requiring Attorney General's consent.
propositions.quote: Subsection (4) provides a screening mechanism for instituting proceedings under s. 117 — prosecutions can proceed only with the consent of the Attorney General.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that subsection (4) requires Attorney General's consent to start proceedings under s. 117.

propositions.text: Unauthorized entry participation may lead to prosecution under s. 117 or inadmissibility under s. 37(1)(b).
propositions.quote: participating in the unauthorized entry of other people into Canada may have two consequences under the IRPA . First, it may result in prosecution and imprisonment and/or substantial fines upon conviction under s. 117 . Second, it may render a person who engages in certain proscribed activities inadmissible to Canada under s. 37(1) (b).

propositions.text: This appeal concerns prosecution under s. 117; inadmissibility under s. 37(1)(b) is addressed in companion appeals.
propositions.quote: The first consequence — prosecution under s. 117 — is the subject of this appeal. The second consequence — inadmissibility to Canada — is the subject of the companion appeals in B010 v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 58, [2015] 3 S.C.R. 704.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains prosecution under s. 117 is at issue here; inadmissibility under s. 37(1)(b) is addressed in companion appeals.

propositions.text: The Charter applies to foreign nationals entering Canada without required documents, engaging s. 7 rights.
propositions.quote: The Charter applies to foreign nationals entering Canada without the required documentation: Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 177. Section 7 of the Charter provides: 7. Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice. As a penal provision with potential sentences up to life imprisonment, it is clear that s. 117 of the IRPA threatens liberty and hence engages s. 7 of the Charter : Re B.C. Motor Vehicle Act, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 486, at p. 492.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Charter applies to foreign nationals without documents and s. 117 engages s. 7 rights due to liberty threat.

propositions.text: Whether s. 117 of the IRPA violates s. 7 of the Charter by threatening liberty contrary to fundamental justice principles.
propositions.quote: The main issue before us is whether s. 117 of the IRPA threatens liberty, protected by s. 7 of the Charter , in a manner contrary to the principles of fundamental justice.

propositions.text: If s. 117 violates s. 7, whether the infringement is justified under s. 1 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: If the answer is yes, a second question arises: Is the infringement justified under s. 1 of the Charter ?

propositions.text: If not justified, what is the appropriate remedy for the constitutional defect in s. 117?
propositions.quote: If the answer to this second question is no, a final question arises: What is the appropriate remedy for the constitutional infirmity in s. 117 ?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies issues: s. 117's s. 7 violation, s. 1 justification, and remedy if unjustified.

propositions.text: s. 117 violates s. 7 because it captures people assisting family or humanitarians outside its purpose, making it overbroad.
propositions.quote: The appellants contend that s. 117 violates s. 7 of the Charter because the provision catches two categories of people outside its purpose — people who assist close family members to come to Canada and humanitarians who assist those fleeing persecution to come to Canada, in each case without required documents.

propositions.text: s. 117 is overbroad, grossly disproportionate, vague, and perpetuates inequality, offending fundamental justice.
propositions.quote: The appellants say that s. 117 is therefore overbroad, contrary to the principles of fundamental justice. They also argue that s. 117 offends the principles of fundamental justice because its impact on liberty is grossly disproportionate to the conduct it targets, because it is unconstitutionally vague, and because it perpetuates inequality.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue s. 117 violates s. 7 by overbroadly capturing family and humanitarian assistance and is disproportionate, vague, and perpetuates inequality.

propositions.text: Overbreadth occurs when law interferes with conduct unrelated to its objective, per Bedford and Carter cases.
propositions.quote: A law is said to violate our basic values by being overbroad when “the law goes too far and interferes with some conduct that bears no connection to its objective”: Canada (Attorney General) v. Bedford, 2013 SCC 72, [2013] 3 S.C.R. 1101, at para. 101. As stated in Bedford, “[o]verbreadth allows courts to recognize that the law is rational in some cases, but that it overreaches in its effect in others”: para. 113; see also Carter v. Canada (Attorney General), 2015 SCC 5, [2015] 1 S.C.R. 331, at para. 85.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains overbreadth means law interferes with conduct unrelated to its objective, citing Bedford and Carter.

propositions.text: Overbreadth analysis involves identifying the law's object and whether it deprives rights in unrelated cases.
propositions.quote: The first step in the overbreadth inquiry is to determine the object of the impugned law. The second step is to determine whether the law deprives individuals of life, liberty or security of the person in cases that do not further that object.

propositions.text: If law deprives s. 7 rights unrelated to its object, it infringes fundamental justice principles.
propositions.quote: To the extent the law does this, it deprives people of s. 7 rights in a manner that infringes the principles of fundamental justice.

paragraphs.summary: The court states overbreadth analysis requires determining the law's object and if it deprives s. 7 rights unrelated to that object.

propositions.text: s. 117 is overbroad as applied to other foreseeable situations, not just appellants' conduct.
propositions.quote: The appellants argue that s. 117 is overbroad, not as it applies to the conduct alleged against them, but as it applies to other reasonably foreseeable situations.

propositions.text: Courts may consider reasonable hypotheticals to assess Charter consistency, per R. v. Nur.
propositions.quote: It is indeed established that a court may consider “reasonable hypotheticals” to determine whether a law is consistent with the Charter : see R. v. Nur, 2015 SCC 15, [2015] 1 S.C.R. 773.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue s. 117 is overbroad in foreseeable cases; courts may consider reasonable hypotheticals per R. v. Nur.

propositions.text: First hypothetical: assisting close family members fleeing to Canada, including mutual assistance among asylum seekers.
propositions.quote: The first scenario the appellants ask us to consider is the situation of a person assisting a close family member to flee to Canada. The appellants cite as examples a mother carrying her small child, or the father of a household taking his family dependants with him aboard a boat. This scenario could also encompass cases of mutual assistance among unrelated asylum-seekers.

propositions.text: Refugees mutually assisting each other is similar to family assistance and is reasonably foreseeable.
propositions.quote: Indeed, refugees mutually assisting one another in their collective flight to safety is not meaningfully different from family members assisting one another and, as showed by the companion case B010, is a reasonably foreseeable situation.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants ask to consider family and mutual refugee assistance as foreseeable scenarios caught by s. 117.

propositions.text: Second hypothetical: humanitarian aid to people fleeing persecution, by individuals or organizations, is a real and historical scenario.
propositions.quote: The second scenario advanced by the appellants is the case of a person who, for humanitarian motives, helps people to flee from persecution. History is replete with examples of people who have aided others to flee persecution for humanitarian reasons. Sometimes the person is acting as an individual. Sometimes the person is a member of an organization devoted to helping people flee lands where they face threats and persecution. Church groups may help undocumented people find refugee protection in Canada: House of Commons Debates, vol. VII, 2nd Sess., 33rd Parl., August 12, 1987, at p. 8002 (Hon. Gerry Weiner, Minister of State (Immigration)). Humanitarian aid to fleeing people is not merely hypothetical; it is a past and current reality.

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue humanitarian aid to persecuted people is a real, historical, and ongoing scenario caught by s. 117.

propositions.text: Overbreadth analysis depends on whether the law's reach exceeds its object, so first determine s. 117's object.
propositions.quote: As discussed, overbreadth analysis turns on whether the reach of the law exceeds its object. The first step is therefore to determine the object of s. 117 .

paragraphs.summary: The court states overbreadth analysis requires determining s. 117's object first.

propositions.text: Crown says s. 117's purpose is to catch all acts assisting undocumented migrants, so not overbroad.
propositions.quote: The Crown argues that the purpose of s. 117 is to catch all acts that in any way assist the entry of undocumented migrants. On this interpretation, s. 117 cannot be overbroad.

propositions.text: Appellants say 'human smuggling' has narrower purpose, making s. 117 overbroad in catching all assistance acts.
propositions.quote: The appellants, by contrast, submit that the offence of “human smuggling” has a narrower purpose than the Crown asserts, making it overbroad in catching all acts of assistance.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown says s. 117 aims to catch all assistance to undocumented migrants; appellants say its purpose is narrower, making it overbroad.

propositions.text: Determining legislative purpose requires considering text, context, purpose statements, and international law.
propositions.quote: As with statutory interpretation, determining legislative purpose requires us to consider statements of legislative purpose together with the words of the provision, the legislative context, and other relevant factors: R. Sullivan, Sullivan on the Construction of Statutes (6th ed. 2014), at pp. 268-87; R. v. Chartrand, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 864, at pp. 879-82. Where legislation is enacted in the context of international commitments, international law may also be of assistance.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains legislative purpose is determined by text, context, purpose statements, and international law.

propositions.text: The court agrees with appellants that s. 117's purpose is narrower than Crown asserts, aimed at combating people smuggling.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I agree with the appellants that the purpose of s. 117 is narrower than that asserted by the Crown. The text of s. 117 is admittedly broad. However, a narrow purpose emerges from (1) the international instruments to which Canada has subscribed; (2) the role of s. 117 in relation to the statute as a whole, in particular s. 37(1) ; (3) the IRPA ’s statements of legislative purpose; (4) the evolution of s. 117 ; and (5) the parliamentary debates. Considering these indicia of purpose, it becomes evident that the true purpose of s. 117 is to combat people smuggling.

propositions.text: The meaning of 'people smuggling' excludes humanitarian conduct, mutual assistance, or family aid, per companion case B010.
propositions.quote: The meaning of “people smuggling”, a term found in s. 37(1) (b) of the IRPA , is the subject of the companion case B010, and excludes mere humanitarian conduct, mutual assistance or aid to family members.

propositions.text: s. 117 violates the Charter by catching conduct outside its purpose, including humanitarian and family assistance.
propositions.quote: I conclude that s. 117 violates the Charter by catching these categories of conduct outside the provision’s purpose.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117's purpose is to combat people smuggling, excluding humanitarian and family aid, and s. 117 violates the Charter by catching such conduct.

propositions.text: Text of s. 117 at relevant time includes prohibitions on organizing or aiding entry without required documents and penalties.
propositions.quote: At the relevant time, the text of s. 117 read as follows: 117. (1) [Organizing entry into Canada] No person shall knowingly organize, induce, aid or abet the coming into Canada of one or more persons who are not in possession of a visa, passport or other document required by this Act. (2) [Penalties — fewer than 10 persons] A person who contravenes subsection (1) with respect to fewer than 10 persons is guilty of an offence and liable (a) on conviction on indictment (i) for a first offence, to a fine of not more than $500,000 or to a term of imprisonment of not more than 10 years, or to both, or (ii) for a subsequent offence, to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to a term of imprisonment of not more than 14 years, or to both; and (b) on summary conviction, to a fine of not more than $100,000 or to a term of imprisonment of not more than two years, or to both. (3) [Penalty — 10 persons or more] A person who contravenes subsection (1) with respect to a group of 10 persons or more is guilty of an offence and liable on conviction by way of indictment to a fine of not more than $1,000,000 or to life imprisonment, or to both. (4) [No proceedings without consent] No proceedings for an offence under this section may be instituted except by or with the consent of the Attorney General of Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court recites the text of s. 117 including prohibitions and penalties for aiding entry without documents.

propositions.text: All agree s. 117(1) text is broad enough to catch family and humanitarian assistance.
propositions.quote: All agree that the text of s. 117(1) is broad enough to catch assistance to close family members and humanitarian assistance.

propositions.text: Overbreadth doctrine recognizes state may use broader means than necessary to achieve legitimate objective.
propositions.quote: However, the doctrine of overbreadth recognizes that sometimes “the State, in pursuing a legitimate objective, uses means which are broader than is necessary to accomplish that objective”: R. v. Heywood, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 761, at p. 792; Bedford, at para. 101; Carter, at para. 85.

propositions.text: Courts must look beyond text to see if Parliament's purpose was narrower due to failures of instrumental rationality.
propositions.quote: The potential for “failures of instrumental rationality”, in which a given law is not a rational means to achieve a legislative objective, requires courts to go further than the text alone, and ask whether other considerations suggest Parliament’s purpose was narrower: Bedford, at para. 107.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117(1) text is broad but overbreadth doctrine requires examining if Parliament's purpose was narrower.

propositions.text: Marginal note and subheading suggest s. 117 targets smuggling in organized crime, not humanitarian or family assistance.
propositions.quote: The marginal note of s. 117 , “Organizing entry into Canada”, read with the subheading “Human Smuggling and Trafficking”, while not to be accorded great weight (see Sullivan, at pp. 465-68), suggests that the provision is aimed at activity in connection with the smuggling of persons in the context of organized crime, as contrasted with providing humanitarian assistance or aiding close family members to enter a country without the required documents.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117's marginal note and subheading suggest focus on organized crime smuggling, not humanitarian or family aid.

propositions.text: Increased penalties for groups of 10+ persons suggest focus on large-scale smuggling operations.
propositions.quote: Sections 117(2) and 117(3) also support the view that Parliament’s intent was to catch smuggling activity in the context of organized crime, rather than humanitarian, mutual or family assistance. These subsections provide for significantly increased sanctions based on the number of persons brought in.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds harsher penalties for large groups indicate focus on organized crime smuggling, not humanitarian or family aid.

propositions.text: Requirement of Attorney General's consent for prosecution suggests s. 117 not intended to convict all caught by broad text.
propositions.quote: Finally, the requirement in s. 117(4) that no prosecution occur without the Attorney General’s consent suggests that s. 117 was not intended to convict everyone who falls within s. 117(1)’s broad ambit, as discussed more fully below.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Attorney General's consent requirement suggests s. 117 not meant to convict all within its broad text.

propositions.text: Legislation presumed to comply with international obligations; courts interpret to reflect international law values.
propositions.quote: As a matter of statutory interpretation, legislation is presumed to comply with Canada’s international obligations, and courts should avoid interpretations that would violate those obligations. Courts must also interpret legislation in a way that reflects the values and principles of customary and conventional international law: R. v. Hape, 2007 SCC 26, [2007] 2 S.C.R. 292, at para. 53; Németh v. Canada (Justice), 2010 SCC 56, [2010] 3 S.C.R. 281, at para. 34.

propositions.text: IRPA s. 3 requires interpretation consistent with Canada's international human rights instruments.
propositions.quote: Section 3 of the IRPA also requires that the IRPA be interpreted in a manner that complies with Canada’s international obligations, including “international human rights instruments to which Canada is signatory”: s. 3(3) (f); see also s. 3(2) (b).

propositions.text: International instruments Canada has subscribed to inform parliamentary purpose behind s. 117.
propositions.quote: The relevant international instruments to which Canada has subscribed should therefore shed light on the parliamentary purpose behind s. 117 of the IRPA .

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislation is presumed to comply with international obligations and IRPA must be interpreted accordingly, informing s. 117's purpose.

propositions.text: IRPA provisions on unauthorized entry assist Canada’s international commitments under Refugee Convention, UN Organized Crime Convention, Smuggling Protocol, and Trafficking Protocol.
propositions.quote: The provisions of the IRPA relating to the fight against the assisting of unauthorized entry of persons to Canada respond to Canada’s international commitments related to these matters in the Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, 189 U.N.T.S. 150 (“Refugee Convention”), the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, 2225 U.N.T.S. 209, the Protocol against the Smuggling of Migrants by Land, Sea and Air, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, 2241 U.N.T.S. 480 (“Smuggling Protocol”), and the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, supplementing the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, 2237 U.N.T.S. 319.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA provisions on unauthorized entry reflect Canada's international commitments under various UN conventions and protocols.

propositions.text: Refugee Convention prohibits penalties for illegal entry by refugees who present themselves promptly and show good cause.
propositions.quote: It provides that states must not impose penalties for illegal entry on refugees who come directly from territories in which their lives or freedom are threatened and who are present on the territory of the foreign state without authorization, “provided they present themselves without delay to the authorities and show good cause for their illegal entry or presence”: art. 31(1).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Refugee Convention forbids penalties for refugees entering illegally if they promptly present themselves and show good cause.

propositions.text: Section 133 IRPA protects foreign nationals entering without documents from illegal entry charges while refugee claims are pending.
propositions.quote: Consistent with this, s. 133 of the IRPA provides that foreign nationals who enter Canada without documents cannot be charged with illegal entry or presence while their refugee claims are pending.

propositions.text: Article 31(1) Refugee Convention grants immunity to genuine refugees entering illegally to seek refuge, including collective illegal entry aid.
propositions.quote: art. 31(1) of the Refugee Convention seeks to provide immunity for genuine refugees who enter illegally in order to seek refuge. For that protection to be effective, the law must recognize that persons often seek refuge in groups and work together to enter a country illegally.

propositions.text: States cannot criminalize refugees solely for aiding others to enter illegally in collective flight to safety under art. 31(1).
propositions.quote: To comply with art. 31(1) , a state cannot impose a criminal sanction on refugees solely because they have aided others to enter illegally in their collective flight to safety.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s.133 IRPA protects undocumented refugees during claims, and art.31(1) Refugee Convention forbids criminalizing collective illegal entry aid by refugees.

propositions.text: Smuggling Protocol aims to combat organized people smuggling, requiring criminalization of smuggling for financial or material benefit.
propositions.quote: The Smuggling Protocol is concerned with stopping the organized crime of people smuggling. It seeks to prevent and combat the smuggling of migrants and to promote cooperation among states to this end, while protecting the rights of smuggled migrants: art. 2. Article 6(1)(a) requires signatory states to adopt measures to establish migrant smuggling as a criminal offence. The Smuggling Protocol includes as a minimum definition for this offence, procuring illegal entry of a person into a state of which the person is not a national or a permanent resident, “in order to obtain, directly or indirectly, a financial or other material benefit”: art. 3 (a).

propositions.text: Smuggling Protocol not directed at family members or humanitarians; includes saving clause preserving other international law rights.
propositions.quote: As I explain in B010, the Smuggling Protocol was not directed at family members or humanitarians: paras. 60 and 68. Furthermore, while the Smuggling Protocol permits subscribing states to enact national laws criminalizing migration-related offences, it includes a “saving clause” that provides that nothing in the Smuggling Protocol “shall affect the other rights, obligations and responsibilities of States and individuals under international law, including international humanitarian law and international human rights law”: art. 19(1).

propositions.text: Broad Crown interpretation of s.117 inconsistent with Smuggling Protocol’s object of protecting smuggled migrants’ rights.
propositions.quote: It would depart from the balance struck in the Smuggling Protocol to allow prosecution for mutual assistance among refugees, family support and reunification, and humanitarian aid. This suggests that the Crown’s broad interpretation of s. 117 ’s purpose is inconsistent with the Smuggling Protocol’s object of protecting the rights of smuggled migrants.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Smuggling Protocol targets organized smuggling for profit, excludes family/humanitarian aid, and Crown’s broad s.117 view conflicts with it.

propositions.text: Interpretation harmonizing Canada’s international commitments supports s.117 targeting organized crime, excluding humanitarian, mutual or family aid.
propositions.quote: I conclude that read together in this way, Canada’s international commitments support the view that the purpose of s. 117 is to permit the robust fight against people smuggling in the context of organized crime. This excludes criminalizing conduct that amounts solely to humanitarian, mutual or family aid.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s.117 aims to fight organized people smuggling, excluding humanitarian, mutual, or family aid, harmonizing international commitments.

propositions.text: Section 117 IRPA must be read harmoniously with other IRPA provisions.
propositions.quote: Section 117 of the IRPA must also be read harmoniously with other provisions of the statute.

paragraphs.summary: The court states s.117 IRPA must be read harmoniously with other IRPA provisions.

propositions.text: Section 117 IRPA is under Part 3 'Enforcement', subheading 'Human Smuggling and Trafficking'; s.118 creates human trafficking offence; s.37(1)(b) renders inadmissible persons engaged in smuggling or trafficking.
propositions.quote: Section 117 of the IRPA falls under Part 3 of the IRPA , entitled “Enforcement”. Section 117 of the IRPA and the provisions that follow it fall under the subheading “Human Smuggling and Trafficking”. Section 118 creates the offence of human trafficking, leaving s. 117 , as noted, to constitute the offence of human smuggling. The only other references in the IRPA to smuggling or trafficking are contained in s. 37(1) (b), which renders inadmissible to Canada a person who has engaged in smuggling or trafficking in persons.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes s.117 IRPA is under enforcement for human smuggling; s.118 covers trafficking; s.37(1)(b) bars inadmissible persons engaged in smuggling or trafficking.

propositions.text: Conduct in s.37(1)(b) IRPA matches Smuggling Protocol’s definition: smuggling for financial/material benefit in transnational crime context.
propositions.quote: As explained in B010, the conduct captured by s. 37(1) (b) is that which is set out in the Smuggling Protocol. In that context, people smuggling only occurs for “financial or other material benefit” and “in the context of transnational crime”.

propositions.text: Reading IRPA inadmissibility and enforcement provisions harmoniously supports s.117 targeting organized smuggling for financial/material benefit, excluding humanitarian, mutual or family aid.
propositions.quote: Reading the inadmissibility and enforcement provisions of the IRPA harmoniously and as part of an integrated scheme therefore supports the view that the purpose of s. 117 is to penalize organizing or abetting illegal entry to Canada through acts knowingly connected to and furthering transnational organized crimes or criminal aims, to obtain, directly or indirectly, a financial or other material benefit. This excludes humanitarian, mutual or family assistance.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s.37(1)(b) IRPA matches Smuggling Protocol’s financial benefit smuggling; s.117 targets organized smuggling, excluding humanitarian or family aid.

propositions.text: Legislative purpose is best found in statements of purpose within the legislation itself.
propositions.quote: The first, “most direct and authoritative evidence” of the legislative purpose of a provision is found in statements of purpose in the legislation itself — whether at the beginning of a statute, in the section in which a provision is found, or in sections providing interpretive guidelines: Sullivan, at pp. 274-76.

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislative purpose is best found in statements of purpose within the legislation itself.

propositions.text: Refugee Convention aims to provide humanitarian refuge while protecting states’ borders.
propositions.quote: In Febles v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 SCC 68, [2014] 3 S.C.R. 431, at paras. 29-30, this Court held that the Refugee Convention has the broad general aim of providing humanitarian refuge for those fleeing persecution while recognizing the need to protect states’ borders.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Febles v. Canada that Refugee Convention balances humanitarian refuge and border protection.

propositions.text: IRPA’s object provisions show both humanitarian refuge and border security goals are important.
propositions.quote: As discussed in B010, the object provisions of the IRPA establish that both of these broad goals are important to the IRPA as well.

propositions.text: Section 117 should be interpreted to balance security concerns and humanitarian aims of IRPA.
propositions.quote: It follows that s. 117 should be interpreted in a balanced way that respects both the security concerns as well as the humanitarian aims of the IRPA .

propositions.text: An interpretation of s.117 catching all assistance to undocumented migrants lets security concerns trump humanitarian aims.
propositions.quote: An interpretation of s. 117 that catches all acts of assistance to undocumented migrants arguably allows security concerns to trump the humanitarian aims of the IRPA .

paragraphs.summary: The court finds IRPA values both security and humanitarian aims; s.117 should balance these, not let security override humanitarian goals.

propositions.text: Crown argues s.117 aims to catch all assistance to undocumented migrants to control borders for security, health, and safety.
propositions.quote: The Crown’s view that the purpose of s. 117 is to catch all acts of assistance to undocumented migrants relies heavily on the fact that among the purposes of the IRPA is to control Canada’s borders to prevent migrants from entering the country illegally, for reasons of security, health and safety.

propositions.text: Crown cites IRPA objectives promoting international justice and security by denying access to security risks and protecting health and safety of Canadians.
propositions.quote: It is reflected in the s. 3(2) (h) objective “to promote international justice and security by denying access to Canadian territory to persons, including refugee claimants, who are security risks or serious criminals”: see also s. 3(1) (i). It is likewise evinced by the aim “to protect the health and safety of Canadians and to maintain the security of Canadian society”: s. 3(2) (g); see also s. 3(1) (h).

paragraphs.summary: The respondent (Crown) argues s.117 aims to catch all assistance to undocumented migrants to protect security, health, and safety.

propositions.text: 1988 amendments to Immigration Act added s.117, aiming to preserve access for genuine protection seekers, control abuse, deter illegal entry assistance, and respond to security concerns.
propositions.quote: A concern with security is also reflected in the specific legislative objects of An Act to amend the Immigration Act and the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, R.S.C. 1985, c. 29 (4th Supp.), the statute which enacted what later became s. 117 of the IRPA (the “1988 amendments”): 1. The Immigration Act is amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 2 thereof, the following heading and section: Purposes of Amendments 2.1 . . . (a) to preserve for persons in genuine need of protection access to the procedures for determining refugee claims; (b) to control widespread abuse of the procedures for determining refugee claims, particularly in light of organized incidents involving large-scale introduction of persons into Canada to take advantage of those procedures; (c) to deter those who assist in the illegal entry of persons into Canada and thereby minimize the exploitation of and risks to persons seeking to come to Canada; and (d) to respond to security concerns, including the fulfilment of Canada’s obligations in respect of internationally protected persons.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes 1988 amendments creating s.117 aimed to preserve genuine protection access, control abuse, deter illegal entry assistance, and address security concerns.

propositions.text: The 1988 statute also recognized humanitarian commitments to preserve access for genuine protection seekers and concern for exploitation and risks to migrants.
propositions.quote: The same statute, however, also recognized humanitarian commitments, including a stated objective “to preserve for persons in genuine need of protection access to the procedures for determining refugee claims” and concern for “exploitation” and risks to persons wishing to come to Canada: s. 1 , adding ss. 2.1(a) and 2.1(c).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the 1988 statute also recognized humanitarian commitments to preserve access and address exploitation risks.

propositions.text: IRPA’s general objects include humanitarian ideals, saving lives, offering protection, and complying with international human rights instruments.
propositions.quote: The IRPA’s general objects further illustrate the importance of its broad humanitarian aims. Section 3(2)(c) speaks of “Canada’s humanitarian ideals”. The stated objects include “saving lives and offering protection to the displaced and persecuted” and “safe haven to persons with a well-founded fear of persecution”: ss. 3(2)(a) and 3(2)(d). Similarly, the objectives include striving to comply with “international human rights instruments to which Canada is signatory”: s. 3(3)(f); see also s. 3(2)(b).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes IRPA’s objects emphasize humanitarian ideals, protection, and compliance with international human rights instruments.

propositions.text: IRPA includes commitment to family reunification as a stated object.
propositions.quote: The IRPA also reveals a commitment to family, through stated objects of facilitating family reunification in Canada: s. 3(2)(f).

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA includes a commitment to family reunification.

propositions.text: Security goals of IRPA do not supplant humanitarian aid and family unity; s.117 targets organized smuggling with criminal dimension, excluding humanitarian, mutual and family aid.
propositions.quote: In sum, while the security goals of the IRPA and the amendment that became s. 117 are important, they do not supplant Canada’s commitment to humanitarian aid and family unity. Both broad aims must be respected. This is accomplished by interpreting s. 117 as targeting organized smuggling operations having a criminal dimension, thereby excluding humanitarian, mutual and family aid.

propositions.text: Crown’s interpretation of s.117 would criminalize trivial humanitarian acts, incompatible with IRPA’s refugee protection objects.
propositions.quote: Under the Crown’s interpretation of s. 117 , a father offering a blanket to a shivering child, or friends sharing food aboard a migrant vessel, could be subject to prosecution. This is incompatible with the refugee protection objects of the IRPA and the amendment that became s. 117 .

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s.117 targets organized smuggling, excluding humanitarian aid; Crown’s broad view would criminalize trivial humanitarian acts, incompatible with IRPA.

propositions.text: Legislative history may assist in determining a provision’s purpose.
propositions.quote: The legislative history of a provision may assist in determining its purpose: Sullivan, at pp. 286-87.

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislative history may help determine a provision’s purpose.

propositions.text: Canada has criminalized assisting undocumented migrants since 1902, initially focused on organizing illegal arrival by rail or ship with little concern for migrants’ plight.
propositions.quote: Canada has had laws criminalizing the assisting of undocumented migrants to enter the country since 1902. Early incarnations of the offence were focused on organizing illegal arrival by rail or ship, with little concern for the plight of the migrants, who were typically expelled: An Act to amend the Immigration Act, S.C. 1902, c. 14, s. 2; Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1906, c. 93, ss. 65 and 66.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Canada has criminalized assisting undocumented migrants since 1902, initially focusing on organizing illegal arrival with little concern for migrants.

propositions.text: In 1919, s.12(4) Immigration Act made it an offence to transport, harbour or conceal prohibited immigrants, with summary conviction penalties; similar offences preserved in 1952 and 1976 Acts.
propositions.quote: In 1919, s. 12(4) of An Act to amend The Immigration Act, S.C. 1919, c. 25, made it an offence to transport into Canada, harbour or conceal the entry of prohibited immigrants. The provision was a summary conviction offence, with a maximum penalty of six months imprisonment and/or fines. Broadly similar offences were preserved in the 1952 and 1976 iterations of the Immigration Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court states 1919 Immigration Act made transporting or harbouring prohibited immigrants an offence with penalties, preserved in later Acts.

propositions.text: In 1988, amendments introduced a new offence criminalizing third party assistance to undocumented migrants, now s. 117 of the IRPA.
propositions.quote: In 1988, “in light of organized incidents involving large-scale introduction of persons into Canada”, amendments introduced a new offence which, with minor changes, is the offence currently found in s. 117 of the IRPA

propositions.text: The offence established maximum penalties based on the number of undocumented entrants, with harsher penalties for 10 or more entrants.
propositions.quote: It criminalized third party assistance to undocumented migrants. In so doing, it established maximum penalties where the number of undocumented entrants was small: six months’ imprisonment and/or $2,000 fines on summary conviction, and five years’ imprisonment and/or $10,000 fines on indictment. By contrast, where the undocumented entrants numbered 10 or more, proceedings were exclusively by indictment, and the maximum penalty was 10 years’ imprisonment and/or fines up to $500,000

propositions.text: The offence included a screening mechanism requiring Attorney General's consent before proceedings under ss. 94.1 or 94.2 could be instituted.
propositions.quote: The offence created in 1988 also included a new screening mechanism: no proceedings could be instituted under ss. 94.1 or 94.2 without the consent of the Attorney General

propositions.text: Greater culpability was attached to large-scale breaches reflecting greater organizational activity.
propositions.quote: Thus, at the inception of what would become s. 117 , greater culpability already attached to large-scale breaches, reflecting greater organizational activity on the part of the accused or others with whom the accused acted in concert.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the 1988 amendments creating s. 117, criminalizing third party assistance to undocumented migrants with penalties based on scale and requiring Attorney General consent.

propositions.text: The current s. 117 was enacted in 2001 as part of the IRPA, preserving penalties and screening mechanisms but increasing maximum penalties.
propositions.quote: The current s. 117 was part of a new comprehensive statute dealing with immigration and refugee protection, the IRPA , enacted in 2001. The offence remained substantially the same as previously, preserving the differing penalties based on scale, and the charge-screening mechanism. However, maximum penalties were significantly increased

propositions.text: Section 121 was added to guide sentencing, considering bodily harm, criminal organization association, profit, and harm to migrants.
propositions.quote: Section 121 provided that in determining the penalty to be imposed under s. 117 , the court was to take into account (1) bodily harm or death to the migrant; (2) association with a criminal organization; (3) profit from the operation; and (4) harm to or degrading treatment of the migrants.

propositions.text: These changes followed the Smuggling Protocol, obliging criminalization of smuggling for financial benefit and aggravating circumstances.
propositions.quote: These changes came on the heels of the adoption of the Smuggling Protocol, which obliged state parties to criminalize the smuggling of migrants done for financial or other material benefit and to adopt legislative measures to establish aggravating circumstances such as harm to and degrading treatment of migrants

propositions.text: The factors in s. 121 reflect links to organized crime, serious crime, and profit indicators.
propositions.quote: The second factor in s. 121 reflected a more significant link between the offensive conduct and organized crime. The first and fourth factors recognized more serious crime. The third factor may be an indicator of either or both.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the 2001 IRPA enactment of s. 117, increasing penalties and adding sentencing factors reflecting organized crime and harm to migrants.

propositions.text: Prohibitions have focused on smuggling tied to organizing illegal entry, not incidental aid.
propositions.quote: the prohibitions have, for over a century, focused on smuggling activity tied to organizing and furthering the illegal entry, not aid merely incidental to it

propositions.text: Revisions increased penalties and targeted organized crime-related smuggling, aligning with international law.
propositions.quote: successive revisions to the provision have coupled increased penalties with more precise targeting of organized crime-related smuggling activity, and the 2001 revision in particular followed in the footsteps of key developments in international law

propositions.text: Section 117 filters out assistance not associated with organized criminal smuggling, like humanitarian acts and mutual aid.
propositions.quote: s. 117 , from its inception in 1988 and as continued and revised by the IRPA in 2001, provided a filter to screen out assistance not associated with organized criminal smuggling, namely innocent humanitarian acts, mutual aid and assistance to family members

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 117 targets organized smuggling, not incidental or humanitarian aid, reflecting evolving penalties and international law.

propositions.text: Legislative statements may supply evidence of a provision's purpose.
propositions.quote: Statements made in the legislature leading up to the enactment of a provision may supply evidence of its purpose

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislative statements can evidence a provision's purpose.

propositions.text: Parliamentary debates show the 1988 offence was motivated by organized large-scale smuggling incidents.
propositions.quote: The parliamentary debates establish that the original enactment of the offence in 1988 was motivated by incidents of organized large-scale smuggling of undocumented migrants by sea

propositions.text: Debates expressed concerns about protecting Canadians, immigration integrity, border control, and refugee safety.
propositions.quote: Concerns were expressed in the debates about protecting the health, safety and security of Canadians and Canadian society, the integrity and efficacy of Canada’s lawful immigration and refugee regimes, and Canada’s ability to control its borders and the domestic and international interests tied to them

propositions.text: Concerns also included protecting genuine refugees and not prosecuting humanitarian groups.
propositions.quote: Concerns were also expressed about the safety and protection of genuine refugees, and not subjecting humanitarian groups to prosecution

propositions.text: Minister Bouchard summarized Parliament's purpose to stop large-scale trafficking and avoid loopholes.
propositions.quote: We are going to put a stop to the large-scale trafficking of illegal migrants by smugglers... We cannot let such individuals escape sanction by adding phrases which create insurmountable problems of proof and create gaps through which the unscrupulous would march

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts 1987 parliamentary debates showing the offence aimed to stop large-scale smuggling while protecting refugees and avoiding loopholes.

propositions.text: Section 117(1) permits prosecution of humanitarian and family assistance due to drafting dilemmas, not intent to capture such persons.
propositions.quote: the reason s. 117(1) of the IRPA permits prosecution of those providing humanitarian assistance to fleeing refugees or assistance to close family members is not because Parliament wanted to capture such persons, but because of a drafting dilemma

propositions.text: Parliament intended to exclude humanitarian and mutual aid from prosecution by requiring Attorney General's consent at prosecution stage.
propositions.quote: Parliament agreed that those offering humanitarian assistance and mutual aid were not meant to be prosecuted under s. 117 of the IRPA . However, instead of legislatively exempting such people from potential criminal liability, it sought to screen them out at the prosecution stage by requiring the Attorney General’s consent to prosecute

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117(1) overreaches due to drafting, but Parliament intended to exclude humanitarian and family aid via Attorney General consent.

propositions.text: 2001 debates echoed concerns that s. 117 might criminalize family and humanitarian aid.
propositions.quote: The debates on the enactment of the IRPA in 2001 echo these preoccupations. Again, members of Parliament expressed concerns that s. 117 might criminalize people who assist family members to come to Canada or people who provide humanitarian aid to asylum-seekers

propositions.text: Government responded that s. 117(4) requiring Attorney General consent would prevent unintended prosecutions.
propositions.quote: The government’s response was that these fears were misplaced because they focused exclusively on s. 117(1) and overlooked s. 117(4) which was expected to prevent these and other unintended prosecutions

propositions.text: Parliamentary debate excerpts show officials explaining s. 117(4) as a safeguard against prosecuting humanitarian workers and family aid providers.
propositions.quote: Mr. Daniel Therrien [General Counsel]: The protection against such prosecutions is in subclause 117(4) , which provides that no prosecution under the smuggling provision can occur without the consent of the Attorney General ... Ms. Joan Atkinson [Assistant Deputy Minister]: ... Subclause 117(4) is what’s in the current act... It is in place ... in the current act, and as Daniel has said, there has been no prosecution of anyone who was involved in trying to help refugees come to Canada. That is the safeguard

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts 2001 debates where government assured s. 117(4) would safeguard humanitarian and family aid from prosecution.

propositions.text: Parliament understood s. 117(1) criminalized humanitarian and family assistance but relied on Attorney General discretion to prevent prosecution.
propositions.quote: These excerpts from the parliamentary debates make it clear that Parliament understood that s. 117(1) criminalized assistance to family members and humanitarian assistance, and was relying on ministerial discretion to prevent prosecution

propositions.text: Officials did not deny s. 117 caught these cases but defended overreach by Attorney General's permission as a safeguard.
propositions.quote: General Counsel Therrien and Assistant Deputy Minister Atkinson did not deny that s. 117 caught these cases, but defended this overreach far beyond any reasonable definition of the targeted smuggling activity on the basis that the Attorney General’s permission under s. 117(4) would be an adequate “safeguard” against inappropriate prosecutions

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament knew s. 117(1) criminalized humanitarian and family aid but relied on Attorney General consent as a safeguard.

propositions.text: Government conceded s. 117(1) was broad enough to catch family and humanitarian assistance but did not intend to prosecute them.
propositions.quote: From the beginning, the government conceded that the words of s. 117(1) had been cast broadly enough to catch family and humanitarian assistance to undocumented migrants... At the same time, the government made it clear that s. 117 was not intended to catch persons aiding family members or providing humanitarian or mutual aid

propositions.text: Government asserted Attorney General authorization under s. 117(4) would alleviate risk of prosecuting such persons.
propositions.quote: The risk would be alleviated, or so the government asserted, by the requirement that the Attorney General authorize prosecutions under s. 117(4) of the IRPA

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes government conceded s. 117(1) was overbroad but relied on Attorney General authorization to prevent wrongful prosecutions.

propositions.text: Section 117's purpose is to criminalize organized crime-related smuggling, not family or humanitarian assistance.
propositions.quote: the purpose of s. 117 is to criminalize the smuggling of people into Canada in the context of organized crime, and does not extend to permitting prosecution for simply assisting family or providing humanitarian or mutual aid to undocumented entrants to Canada

propositions.text: A broad punitive goal prosecuting persons unconnected to organized crime is inconsistent with Parliament's purpose.
propositions.quote: A broad punitive goal that would prosecute persons with no connection to and no furtherance of organized crime is not consistent with Parliament’s purpose as evinced by the text of s. 117 read together with Canada’s international commitments, s. 117 ’s role within the IRPA , the IRPA ’s objects, the history of s. 117 , and the parliamentary debates

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117 aims to criminalize organized crime smuggling, not family or humanitarian aid, consistent with Parliament's purpose.

propositions.text: Whether s. 117 goes too far and interferes with conduct unrelated to its objective.
propositions.quote: I now turn to the scope of s. 117 of the IRPA to see whether it “goes too far and interferes with some conduct that bears no connection to its objective”

paragraphs.summary: The court raises the issue whether s. 117 overreaches by interfering with conduct unrelated to its objective.

propositions.text: Section 117(1) is unambiguous and admits no ambiguity in its scope.
propositions.quote: The scope of s. 117(1) is plain. The provision admits of no ambiguity

propositions.text: Parliament knew s. 117(1) was overbroad, catching humanitarian, mutual and family assistance, but relied on Attorney General consent to prevent prosecution.
propositions.quote: Parliament itself understood when it enacted s. 117 that the provision’s reach exceeded its purpose by catching those who provide humanitarian, mutual and family assistance to asylum-seekers coming to Canada, but argued that this overbreadth was not a problem because the Attorney General would not permit the prosecution of such people

propositions.text: Interpreting s. 117(1) to exclude humanitarian, mutual or family assistance would violate statutory interpretation rules and ignore legislative debates.
propositions.quote: We cannot avoid the overbreadth problem by interpreting s. 117(1) as not permitting prosecution of persons providing humanitarian, mutual or family assistance... To adopt this suggestion would violate the rule of statutory interpretation that the meaning of the words of the provision should be read in their “grammatical and ordinary sense”... It would also require us to ignore statements from the legislative debate record suggesting Parliament knew in advance that the provision was overbroad

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117(1) unambiguous and overbroad, catching humanitarian and family aid, and cannot be narrowly interpreted to exclude them.

propositions.text: Section 117(1) criminalizes conduct unrelated to its objective, raising overbreadth concerns.
propositions.quote: I conclude that s. 117(1) appears to criminalize some conduct that bears no relation to its objective, raising the spectre that s. 117 as a whole is overbroad

propositions.text: Whether Attorney General's consent under s. 117(4) saves s. 117 from overbreadth by narrowing its scope.
propositions.quote: The remaining question is whether the requirement under s. 117(4) that the Attorney General authorize prosecution saves s. 117 from the charge or overbreadth by effectively narrowing the scope of s. 117(1)

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117(1) overbroad and questions if Attorney General consent under s. 117(4) cures this.

propositions.text: Section 117(4) does not cure overbreadth; ministerial discretion does not negate criminalization beyond Parliament's object.
propositions.quote: In my view, s. 117(4) does not cure the overbreadth problem created by s. 117(1). Ministerial discretion, whether conscientiously exercised or not, does not negate the fact that s. 117(1) criminalizes conduct beyond Parliament’s object

propositions.text: Persons providing family, mutual or humanitarian assistance face risk of prosecution and imprisonment under s. 117(1).
propositions.quote: So long as the provision is on the books, and so long as it is not impossible that the Attorney General could consent to prosecute, a person who assists a family member or who provides mutual or humanitarian assistance to an asylum-seeker entering Canada faces a possibility of imprisonment

propositions.text: Prosecutorial discretion does not excuse constitutional breaches.
propositions.quote: as this Court unanimously noted in R. v. Anderson, 2014 SCC 41... “prosecutorial discretion provides no answer to the breach of a constitutional duty”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117(4) does not fix overbreadth; prosecutorial discretion cannot excuse constitutional breaches.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal viewed problem as administrative law issue about Attorney General's discretion under s. 117(4).
propositions.quote: Implicit in the Court of Appeal’s position is that the problem of humanitarian workers or family members prosecuted under s. 117 of the IRPA is a problem of administrative law, and that if a constitutional attack is to be made, it should be made against improper exercise of the Attorney General’s duty under s. 117(4) not to prosecute such persons

propositions.text: The court disagrees, noting s. 117 allows prosecution of such persons and judicial review of discretion is limited and may be undesirable.
propositions.quote: I cannot agree... judicial review of such discretion is not currently available, and there are good reasons why it may not be desirable... judicial oversight of Crown decisions whether to prosecute puts at risk the discrete roles of different actors in our adversarial system

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the Court of Appeal's view that the issue is administrative law, noting limited judicial review and risks to adversarial roles.

propositions.text: Judicial review of Attorney General's prosecution decisions under s. 117(4) may have undesirable consequences for other federal statutes with similar clauses.
propositions.quote: judicial review of the Attorney General’s decision to authorize prosecution under s. 117(4) may have undesirable consequences for other federal statutes in which a similar clause is present

propositions.text: Judicial review does not resolve s. 117(1)'s constitutional non-conformity.
propositions.quote: At this point, it suffices to note that judicial review does not answer the constitutional non-conformity of s. 117(1)

paragraphs.summary: The court notes judicial review of Attorney General decisions may have negative effects and does not fix s. 117(1)'s constitutional issues.

propositions.text: Section 117 of the IRPA is overbroad.
propositions.quote: I conclude that s. 117 of the IRPA is overbroad

propositions.text: Whether the overbreadth is justified under s. 1 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: The remaining issue is whether this overbreadth is justified under s. 1 of the Charter as a reasonable measure in a free and democratic society

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 117 is overbroad and raises the issue of justification under s. 1 of the Charter.

propositions.text: Appellants assert s. 117 violates s. 7 by gross disproportionality, vagueness, and equality principles.
propositions.quote: some of the appellants assert that s. 117 offends s. 7 by depriving persons of liberty in a manner that violates the principles of fundamental justice against gross disproportionality and vagueness. They also claim that equal treatment under the law is a principle of fundamental justice within the meaning of s. 7 , and that s. 117 violates it

propositions.text: Given s. 117 is overbroad, the court finds it unnecessary to consider these additional arguments.
propositions.quote: In view of my conclusion that s. 117 is overbroad, I find it unnecessary to consider these arguments

paragraphs.summary: The appellants argue s. 117 violates s. 7 by gross disproportionality, vagueness, and equality, but the court declines to consider these further.

propositions.text: The s. 1 justification test is from R. v. Oakes, requiring pressing and substantial objective.
propositions.quote: The test to determine whether infringement of a right may be constitutionally justified under s. 1 of the Charter was set out in R. v. Oakes... The first step of the s. 1 analysis asks whether the Crown has demonstrated a pressing and substantial objective

propositions.text: The broad purpose of s. 117 is to combat organized crime-related people smuggling without criminalizing family, mutual, or humanitarian aid.
propositions.quote: The broad purpose of s. 117 of the IRPA is to combat organized crime-related people smuggling, without criminalizing family assistance, mutual aid or humanitarian aid to asylum-seekers coming to Canada. This objective is clearly pressing and substantial

paragraphs.summary: The court states the s. 1 test from Oakes and finds s. 117's purpose is pressing and substantial.

propositions.text: Not all applications of s. 117 are rationally connected to its objective, but some are, satisfying rational connection stage.
propositions.quote: Not all applications of s. 117 are rationally connected to the legislative object... However, since other applications of s. 117 are rationally connected to the legislative object, this suffices to satisfy the rational connection stage of the analysis

propositions.text: Rational connection requires a connection, not complete correspondence, per Heywood.
propositions.quote: A rational connection, not a complete rational correspondence, is all this branch of Oakes requires

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117 partially rationally connected to its objective, satisfying the rational connection step under Oakes.

propositions.text: The third step of s. 1 analysis asks if the law is tailored to its objective, citing R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd.
propositions.quote: The third step of the s. 1 analysis asks whether the offending law is tailored to its objective: R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd., [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713.

propositions.text: A law that goes too far challenges minimal impairment requirement under s. 1 analysis.
propositions.quote: Evidently, where a law goes too far, it is a challenge to satisfy minimal impairment.

propositions.text: In Heywood, Cory J. found the law overly broad and failing minimal impairment under s. 1 analysis.
propositions.quote: In Heywood, Cory J. concluded (at p. 803) that “for the same reasons that [the law] is overly broad, it fails the minimal impairment branch of the s. 1 analysis”.

propositions.text: The record here shows that overbreadth does not always mean failure of minimal impairment.
propositions.quote: The record here shows why that will not always necessarily be the case.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 1 minimal impairment step, cites Heywood's finding of overbreadth failing minimal impairment, but notes overbreadth does not always fail.

propositions.text: The Crown argues that despite overbreadth, the provision is minimally impairing as no better alternative existed.
propositions.quote: The Crown’s position appears to be that even though the provision is overbroad, it is nevertheless minimally impairing, because although imperfect, there was no better alternative.

propositions.text: Government recognized the provision would criminalize unintended conduct but enacted it to avoid loopholes.
propositions.quote: the government recognized in advance that the provision would catch conduct it did not intend to criminalize. However, Parliament nevertheless enacted an overbroad provision because it was concerned that wording exempting this conduct would create unacceptable loopholes.

propositions.text: Section 1 requires demonstrable justification for rights limitations, not bare claims, citing Oakes.
propositions.quote: Section 1 of the Charter does not allow rights to be limited on the basis of bare claims, but requires the Crown to provide a demonstrable justification for inconsistencies with Charter rights: Oakes, at pp. 136-37.

propositions.text: The Crown has not met its burden under s. 1 to justify the provision's overbreadth.
propositions.quote: The Crown has not satisfied its burden under s. 1 .

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues minimal impairment despite overbreadth; the court finds the Crown failed to justify the provision under s. 1.

propositions.text: Section 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 states the Constitution is supreme and inconsistent laws are of no force or effect.
propositions.quote: Section 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 provides: 52. (1) The Constitution of Canada is the supreme law of Canada, and any law that is inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution is, to the extent of the inconsistency, of no force or effect.

propositions.text: Section 117 is of no force or effect to the extent it is inconsistent with the Charter.
propositions.quote: It follows that s. 117 is of no force or effect to the extent of its inconsistency with the Charter .

paragraphs.summary: The court states s. 52(1) makes inconsistent laws invalid and that s. 117 is invalid to the extent it conflicts with the Charter.

propositions.text: The inconsistency proven is s. 117's overbreadth regarding humanitarian aid, mutual aid among asylum-seekers, and family assistance.
propositions.quote: The extent of the inconsistency that has been proven is the overbreadth of s. 117 in relation to three categories of conduct: (1) humanitarian aid to undocumented entrants, (2) mutual aid amongst asylum-seekers, and (3) assistance to family entering without the required documents.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 117 overbroad regarding humanitarian aid, mutual aid, and family assistance.

propositions.text: The appellants ask the Court to strike down s. 117 entirely.
propositions.quote: The appellants ask the Court to strike s. 117 down in its entirety.

propositions.text: Section 117 has been replaced since the alleged offences occurred.
propositions.quote: Section 117 , as it was at the time of the alleged offences, has been replaced.

propositions.text: The preferable remedy is to read down s. 117 to exclude humanitarian, mutual, or family assistance conduct.
propositions.quote: I conclude that the preferable remedy is to read down s. 117 as not applicable to persons who give humanitarian, mutual or family assistance.

propositions.text: This remedy reconciles s. 117 with the Charter and preserves the human smuggling prohibition.
propositions.quote: This remedy reconciles the former s. 117 with the requirements of the Charter while leaving the prohibition on human smuggling for the relevant period in place.

propositions.text: The remedy aligns with this Court's guidance in Schachter v. Canada.
propositions.quote: This remedy is consistent with the guidance this Court gave in Schachter v. Canada, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 679.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant seeks full repeal of s. 117; the court prefers reading it down to exclude humanitarian and family aid, consistent with Charter and precedent.

propositions.text: The appeals are allowed and s. 117 is read down to exclude humanitarian and mutual aid to conform with the Charter.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeals and read down s. 117 of the IRPA , as it was at the time of the alleged offences, as not applying to persons providing humanitarian aid to asylum-seekers or to asylum-seekers who provide each other mutual aid (including aid to family members), to bring it in conformity with the Charter .

propositions.text: Charges are remitted for trial on the basis of the read-down s. 117.
propositions.quote: The charges are remitted for trial on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeals, reads down s. 117 to exclude humanitarian and mutual aid, and remits charges for trial accordingly.
